rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabad means hardship and toil; although the verse can include all humans, Islahi says its immediate addressees are the Ishmaelites, especially Quraysh.
rows.anchor: means “hardship” and “toil.” Though the word is general to include all human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recalls Ishmael’s settlement in a barren, insecure land, where life was nomadic, exposed, and dependent on protecting people and herds.
rows.anchor: People lived here like nomads and their life was full of toil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s prayer, the House’s sanctity and custodianship, and safe trade journeys brought abundant sustenance and changed Quraysh’s toil into ease.
rows.anchor: their life of toil and struggle transformed into a life of ease and comfort

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh became vain in their comfort, treating wealth as birthright and claiming freedom to spend without God or the Prophet’s interference.
rows.anchor: they contended that what they received was their birthright and they could expend it in any manner they wanted to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an recalls the House’s history to warn Quraysh that rebellion after divine favors invites their destruction.
rows.anchor: if they became rebellious after receiving these favours from God, they would only be inviting their doom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham settled Ishmael in barren Makkah to protect him from a polytheistic environment.
rows.anchor: could be protected from the environment of polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham built the House as a worship center for his descendants and prayed that people’s hearts would turn toward it and them.
rows.anchor: built the House of God in this land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Makkah was barren and unsafe, Abraham also prayed for abundant food and security for its inhabitants.
rows.anchor: food provisions and become safe and secure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s present status and riches came from Abraham’s prayer and the House’s blessings, not their planning or tribal entitlement.
rows.anchor: status and riches the Quraysh had at the time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The favor is conditional on worship, fulfilling the House’s purpose, and believing the sent Prophet; otherwise Quraysh will lose it.
rows.anchor: they will remain in this status; otherwise all this will be confiscated from them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah Quraysh says continued blessings and custodianship require worshipping the House’s Lord.
rows.anchor: if they want to keep receiving the blessings of the House of God, the only way is to worship the God of this House

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s knowledge of Makkah’s history should prevent them from mistaking current affluence for immunity; God can destroy them, especially while they neglect Abraham’s purpose.
rows.anchor: there is no reason for those who know the early history of this area to be misled by their current affluence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conceit that wealth and status were self-earned or a birthright leaves people unwilling to spend for God and indifferent to Him and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: spend in the way of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To excuse miserliness, such people recite their many personal and collective expenses and challenge callers to say how much more they should give.
rows.anchor: long list of expenditures and try to prove to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression mālan lubadā means a great amount of wealth.
rows.anchor: means “a great amount of wealth.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees the truth behind their boast: they spend nothing yet claim generosity, and their supposed spending will be fully exposed.
rows.anchor: no one is observing their generosity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth has so distracted the addressees that they have not properly used their eyes to notice the needy around them.
rows.anchor: blessed them with two eyes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exhortation is included in the believer’s obligation; without it, the virtuous deed remains incomplete.
rows.anchor: is included in his obligation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tongue is a powerful, sharp-edged weapon, so its use should be deliberate and purposeful.
rows.anchor: It is a sharp-edged sword

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Virtue requires both practice and exhortation; urging others is every society member’s duty and will be accounted for, a theme developed at 103:1-3.
rows.anchor: Urging others to adopt virtue is the responsibility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two lips protect the valuable, powerful tongue like a sheath for a sword, so it should be used for its proper purpose rather than trivialities.
rows.anchor: The principle is that the more valuable and capable of producing profound, effective and far-reaching results a thing is the more it is protected and safeguarded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God also guides people to the two moral paths, described in 76:3 and more explicitly in 91:7-10.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has also guided him regarding the two paths

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human beings know good and evil; wrongdoing stems from being overcome by emotions despite that awareness, not from ignorance.
rows.anchor: knowing full well that he is committing evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The addressees fail to acknowledge divine favors: intellect, speech, and guidance should move them to compassion, service, and seeking nearness to God, but greed and wealth restrain them.
rows.anchor: they did not have the courage to do so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAqabah means a steep path and iqtihām means climbing it or undertaking difficulty; here they denote compassionate service to creation and service to God, which demand sacrifice.
rows.anchor: virtue which relate to showing sympathy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Higher aims require redirecting the self away from immediate rewards, while trivial acts offer easy, immediate benefit; Matthew 7:13-14 and a Muslim report about Paradise’s hardships illustrate this.
rows.anchor: Paradise is surrounded by hardships

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question magnifies the steep path: rites alone do not make people God’s intimates; they need courage to climb it, and the next verses name the deeds required.
rows.anchor: Such a question is posed to express the majesty or dread of something

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Freeing a slave is the first virtue named, universally recognized as good and placed at the forefront of human service from the Qur’an’s earliest preaching; the Qur’an later promoted slavery’s gradual elimination.
rows.anchor: Liberating a slave and making an effort that others also do so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feeding the poor has the broader sense of meeting all their needs, and its merit rises during famine.
rows.anchor: means to fulfil all the needs of such people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The famine qualifier strengthens the appeal because feeding the poor is especially valuable in famine conditions.
rows.anchor: in days of famine its value increases greatly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every orphan deserves help, but a relative who is orphaned is especially worthy of support.
rows.anchor: every orphan deserves help; however

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about an indigent in the dust intensifies the picture of destitution and need.
rows.anchor: the case of the qualifying phrase

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sensitive people who notice the downtrodden should do the stated virtuous deeds and also join believers who counsel patience and sympathy.
rows.anchor: call people to show patience and to be sympathetic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Failure to do the deeds and join the faithful reflects an obstacle to moral and spiritual growth that the person has not overcome.
rows.anchor: they have not been able to overcome

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience accompanies sympathy because virtuous deeds oppose inner desire and feel like climbing a slope; ṣabr means perseverance and steadfastness needed for that effort.
rows.anchor: Those who are devoid of this quality lack valour and bravery

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right-hand faction’s fate is left unstated but inferred as residence in Paradise’s upper floors, contrasted with the wrongdoers’ sealed fire.
rows.anchor: The suppressed words are to the effect: they shall reside in the upper floors of the buildings of Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although maymanah can mean right-hand side, Islahi prefers blessed or fortunate because the term contrasts with mashʾamah, misfortune; the distinction is only literal.
rows.anchor: it is mentioned in contrast to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right- and left-hand names also reflect the fortunate and unfortunate, since the righteous receive accounts in their right hands and the impious in their left, as in al-Ḥāqqah.
rows.anchor: the pious will be given their account in their right hands and the impious will be given their account in their left hands

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muʾṣadah depicts fire enveloping the wrongdoers with its doors shut on them.
rows.anchor: The Fire shall close in on them

none: Closing gratitude, date, and place only; no further interpretive point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Balad warned Quraysh that Makkah’s prosperity came through Abraham’s prayer and the House, so they must not become arrogant; Shams warns what follows if they persist.
rows.anchor: warned of their fate should they persist in their arrogance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world appears to contain opposing forces, yet God keeps them within limits and in harmony; their accord preserves the universe.
rows.anchor: the Almighty does not allow these opposing forces to exceed their limits

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul mirrors the larger world: God inspires good and evil, inclines it to good and against evil, and requires it to preserve balance; unchecked evil leads to arrogance and disorder.
rows.anchor: inclined it towards good and made it hate evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tolerates arrogance and disorder only while expedient, then destroys those whose collective existence threatens the world; Thamūd exemplify the warning to Quraysh.
rows.anchor: When these things cross the bounds, the Almighty destroys them and cleanses His world from people whose existence becomes dangerous for it in their collective capacity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh are warned that if they adopt Thamūd’s arrogant attitude, God will seize them and no one can help.
rows.anchor: no one would be able to help them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night are complementary phenomena; their apparent oppositions in appearance, temperament, and effects serve in harmony.
rows.anchor: which act in complement to each other

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier sūrahs used this complementarity for arguments about monotheism and the Day of Judgement; here the focus is how the apparent opposites work together.
rows.anchor: the specific aspect which is brought in focus is that although the sun and the moon and the night and day are seemingly opposing to one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cosmic order prevents the sun or moon from intruding on the other’s appointed time and keeps day and night within their roles, as 36:40 says.
rows.anchor: Neither does the sun interfere with movement of the moon nor does the moon push itself to appear before its appointed time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Harmony among opposites sustains the universe; their obedience to limits teaches people to stay within God’s bounds, since exceeding them creates disorder God will not tolerate.
rows.anchor: they too should lead a life within the bounds set for them by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky’s structure and scale testify to its Maker’s power, wisdom, and providence; those qualities require that people be judged and rewarded or punished, lest creation be purposeless.
rows.anchor: signs here and not of His own self

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For mā in the sky and earth oaths, Islahi prefers the verbal-noun reading over the relative reading, which would refer to God rather than the created signs sworn by.
rows.anchor: it does not merely convert a verb into a verbal noun, it also directs our attention to the majesty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mā verbal-noun construction evokes the grandeur, wisdom, and creativity of the action; the sky phrase thus invokes its amazing structure and all its wonders as signs.
rows.anchor: the sky and its amazing structure bear witness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth’s being spread out similarly contains the wonders and details highlighted at 88:20; mā invites reflection on them, with a subtle distinction from kayfa left beyond this discussion.
rows.anchor: the earth, how it has been spread out?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul itself witnesses its Maker’s purpose: awareness of good and evil entails adopting good and avoiding evil; success is purification and failure is sin, so denying accountability contradicts this witness.
rows.anchor: the awareness of good and evil is found in it. Obviously, the reason for giving him this awareness is that man should adopt good and shield himself from evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because al-nafs lacks the definite article, it can convey magnitude, multitude, or scarcity; Islahi prefers magnitude to highlight the soul’s remarkable wisdom and abilities.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, here it connotes magnitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā sawwāhā is also a verbal noun pointing to the soul’s artistry; such a highly endowed creation must have a purpose and face accountability.
rows.anchor: highly gifted without a purpose

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taswiyah denotes creation’s final stage, as in 87:2; the perfected soul’s capacities make it a witness that humans have responsibilities and answer to God.
rows.anchor: here it is not merely the initial stage of the creation of the human soul which is referred to in this oath, its final stage is also in consideration
